Cheat sheets and review notes for CBE 150B, mass transfer and separation processes (UC Berkeley). 24 handwritten pages: pages 1–4 are the full-size draft of the final exam sheet, pages 5–9 the compact final sheet, and the rest midterm cheat sheets and review notes.

Pages 1–4 — full-size draft of the final sheet

These pages carry the same formulas as the compact final sheet on pages 5–6 (drying, thermodynamics, flash, absorption and stripping, binary and multicomponent distillation), written larger. Only the items that do not also appear on pages 5–6 are transcribed here; see the scans for the rest.

  • Drying: T(°R)=T(°F)+459.67; heat-transfer coefficients h=0.0204G0.8 [J/m²·s·K] (parallel flow), G=ρv [kg/m²·h]; h=1.17G0.37 (perp. flow).
  • Distillation energy balance: V=Vˉ+VF​ (partially vaporized); (L+D)=VB​⋅B+VF​; D(R+1)=VB​⋅B+VF​; QR​=QR​−VF​; QR​=QR​(1−QR​VF​​)=QR​(1−D(R+1)VF​​) (VF​/F for the flash).
  • Cost plot: (sketch: cost vs. R — capital cost falls from Rmin​, operating cost rises, total minimum at (Rmin​R​)opt​=1.3.)
  • Assumptions for stripper/absorber: (1) constant L, V; (2) no air dissolved in L or L evaporated in air; (3) ideal gas for air.
  • Stage (count the reboiler as 0); tray (count the reboiler as 1); partial reboiler → 1st stage is R; partial condenser → last stage is R [?].
  • Membrane separation (new formulas):
    • Porous — gas: Ni​=Plm​Dei​​Cm​​(Pi0​​−PiL​​); Cm​=RTρ​; Dei​​=τε​[Di​1​+DKi​​1​1​]; permeance ⇒Pmi​​=PDei​​Cm​​
    • Porous — liquid: Ni​=lm​Dei​​​(Ci0​​−CiL​​); Dei​​=τεDi​Kri​​​; Kri​​=[1−dp​dmi​​​]4; permeance: τεDi​Kri​​​
    • Non-porous — gas: Ni​=lm​Hi​Di​​(Pi0​​−PiL​​); Hi​=Pi0​Ci0​​=PiL​CiL​​; Pmi​​=Hi​Di​
    • Non-porous — liquid: Ni​=lm​Di​​(Ci0​−CiL​)=lm​Ki​Di​​(Ci0′​−CiL′​); Ki​=Ci0′​Ci0​​=CiL′​CiL​​; Pmi​​=Ki​Di​
  • Multicomponent distillation: Fenske (Nmin​) → Underwood (Rmin​) → Gilliland (real N & R); Underwood class I (all components distribute) or class II (only LK & HK distribute). α=yi​/xi​; ↑α means it’s more volatile (lower Teq).

Multicomponent distillation

  1. Specify splits (LK, HK)
  2. Estimate splits of non-key components
  3. Determine column pressure & type of condenser (dew point & bubble point)
  4. Flash the feed @ column pressure (adiabatic flash)
  5. Calculate Nmin​ (Fenske)
  6. Calculate splits of non-key
  7. Calculate (R∞​)min​ (Underwood)
  8. Calculate N, R (Gilliland)
  9. Calculate feed location (Kirkbride)
  10. Condenser & reboiler duties

Class I → narrow-boiling-range mixture, low degree of separation.

Nmin​=logαij​log{(xi,B​)(xi,D​)​(xj,D​)(xj,B​)​}​=logαm​log{dj​di​​bi​bj​​}​;αm​=[(αij​)N​(αij​)1​]1/2

Liquid–liquid extraction (LLE)

  • Type II: solute & solvent very miscible; requires a high flow rate of solvent (S/F). Type I: solute & solvent more miscible than type II. (sketches: ternary diagrams with the two-phase dome; heating from T=35 °C to T=45 °C shrinks the dome.)
  • (sketch: a mixer–settler — carrier/feed and solvent enter the mixer, the separator gives raffinate and extract; a countercurrent cascade of stages 1…N with raffinates R1​…RN​ and extracts E1​…EN​, solvent S entering at stage N.)
  • Selectivity=Kcarrier​Ksolute​​=(xW​)E​/(xW​)R​(xAC​)E​/(xAC​)R​​ (W = carrier, Ac​ = solute)
  • F+S=M=E+R (same lines on the ternary diagram)

(sketch: ternary diagram with solute at the apex, solvent (S) and carrier corners; the feed F, mixture point M, Emin​, RN​ and the difference point Pmin​.)

  1. Finding Smin​ (min. solvent flow rate):
    • Find E using the tie line through F to the S–RN​ line
    • Connect Emin​ & RN​
    • Find M using the graphical method: MS​=SFMF​ or FS​=MSMF​ (M=100+S)
  2. Find stages:
    • Given S, F → we can find M: (xA​)S​S+(xA​)F​F=(xA​)M​M
    • Find the intersection of A and the S–F line to find M
    • Connect M & R to the other side to find E1​ (this is the starting E1​)
    • Extend S–R & E–F to meet @ P
    • Now the new R1​ is found using the tie line, and R is connected to P to find E2​
    • Repeat steps until the tie line crosses R (given) & then count stages

Converting LLE to McCabe–Thiele: (sketch: ternary diagram with tie lines up to the plait point, mapped to a y–x curve.) y–x from eq. tie-line data; E–R (points through P) make up the operating line.

Drying

  • cp​=1.005+1.88H​ — heat capacity [=] kJ/kg dry·K: the conc. of air plus how much the humidity changes the cp​ (heat capacity increases w/ water present)

  • T−Ts​H−H~s​​=λH2​O​−cp,in​​​ } energy needed to achieve a certain level of drying ↳ if you are evap. something then the outlet should be cooler. Always logic check.

  • X=Wdry​Wtot​−Wdry​​​; rate of vaporization R=−AWdry​​dtdX​​; boundary cond. q=k(T−Tsat​) (doesn’t have to be sat.); R=ΔHvap​q​

Governing equation (diffusion limits evaporation because water has to travel to the surface — finite slab drying): ∂t∂X​=Dt​∂y2∂2X​ (sketch: a slab of half-thickness y1​); (1) X(y,t=0)=X; (2) X(y=y1​,t)=0 (symmetry); (3) ∂y∂X​​y=0​=0.

Answer: X1​X(t)​=π28​exp(−Dt​(2y1​π​)2t)​

Transcriber’s note: BC (2) is labelled “symmetry” in the original, but symmetry is BC (3), ∂X/∂y=0 at y=0; BC (2) is the dry surface.

Time to dry from Xc​ to Xf​:

  • t=A(λH2​O​k(T−Tw​)​)Wdry​​(Xc​−Xf​) — A = area of plate, k = mass-transfer coefficient (depends on the mass-transfer coefficient)
  • t=π2Dt​4y12​​ln(π2Xf​8Xc​​) — Dt​ = diffusivity of water in the slab

(sketch: rate of drying vs. X — bound water rising linearly to Xc​, then a constant-rate plateau (unbound water, “where you have a puddle of water on top and that is evaporating”).) The falling part is the rate when water has to diffuse; bound water is mass-transfer limited because it has to diffuse to the surface to evaporate.

Absorption/stripping

  • Absorber (gas to liquid); stripper (liq. to gas).
  • ϕA​=vn+1​v1​​; ϕS​=ln+1​l1​​ (l, v = the component that you are trying to remove); ϕA​ = fraction not removed; ϕA​=1 (worst separation).

  • Count from the stream that is clean ↳ we label a stream based on whatever stage it leaves.

  • This is useful in case L0​ & Ln​ are not the same (as an absorber would gain mass) ↓ therefore we do it only in terms of the solvent (taking out the solutes from the equation):

Page 17 — “Heating & Mixing Sh*t”

Absorption/stripping — two ways to solve this:

  • (a) Graphical: McCabe–Thiele (any VLE)
  • (b) Analytical: Kremser (assume dilute-solution VLE) ↳ Henry’s law & constant L/V

(a) Graphical (sketch: an absorber — inlet solvent L0​, x0​ at the top (stage 1), vapor V1​, y1​ out; inlet gas VN+1​, yN+1​ at the bottom (stage N), liquid LN​, xN​ out; around stage n: Ln−1​, xn−1​ down and Vn​, yn​ up above; Ln​, xn​ and Vn+1​, yn+1​ below.)

  • Overall material balance (@ the ends): yN+1​VN+1​+x0​L0​=y1​V1​+xN​LN​
  • Balance from 1→n stages (n = stages from the top ≠ N, the total no. of stages): yn+1​Vn+1​+x0​L0​=y1​V1​+xn​Ln​
  • Rearranging this equation:
yn+1​=Vn+1​y1​V1​+xn​Ln​−x0​L0​​=y1​Vn+1​V1​​+xn​Vn+1​Ln​​−x0​Vn+1​L0​​⇒yn+1​=gradient(Vn+1​Ln​​)​​xn​+intercept(y1​−Vn+1​L0​​x0​)​​→this becomes the operating line

VLE & VL​ is constant (ideal stages): yN​=(VL​)xN​+(y1​−VL​x0​).

Small technicality: we define yA​=total moles of gas mixturemoles of solute A (in gas)​. However, the gas is in two different mixtures ∴ yA​=[moles of carrier gas+mole of solute B]A in gas​ ∴ y1​=Y1​=1−yA​yA​​. Similarly, X1​=1−yB​yB​​.

Therefore the final equations we get:

YN+1​=(VL​)XN​+(Y1​−VL​X0​)

Steps: (1) draw the eq. line from Henry’s law; (2) draw the operating line (YN+1​, X1​, VL​, XN​ are known).

Page 18 — liquid–liquid extraction

(sketch: a mixer–separator — carrier/feed and solvent in; raffinate and extract out.)

  • → The “carrier” carries the “solute”; → this is what you need to extract (the solute from the carrier).
  • The raffinate carries the unwanted carrier/feed (and some small amounts of remaining solute).
  • The extract carries the desired solute and some amount of carrier that might have slightly dissolved.

(sketch: a ternary diagram with solute B at the top, solvent C at the bottom left, carrier/feed A at the bottom right.)

Finding M graphically: F+S=M=E+R (F, S, M lie on the same line; M, E, R lie on the same line — “sht going in = sht coming out”).
